These mistakes cost you search rankings and AI visibility.

articles.author: bingkahu
articles.description:
It is February 16th. Today, we are playing with perception. Your task is to create a seamless, infinitely scrolling background or list—but there is a catch that might make your brain loop.
Create a UI element that scrolls forever in one direction without the user ever seeing a "jump" or a "seam" where the loop restarts.
NO JavaScript Allowed : You cannot use scroll, requestAnimationFrame, or any script-based positioning.
Pure CSS/HTML only : Use @keyframes and transform to handle the movement.
Perfect Loop : The animation must be perfectly seamless. If the user can see it "snap" back to the start, the illusion is broken!
The content should move at a constant speed. Whether it's a marquee of logos, a parallax starfield, or a list of items, it must look like a single, never-ending stream.
Pro Tip : Doubling your content and using a translateX(-50%) or translateY(-50%) trick is usually the cleanest way to hide the seam.
Drop your CodePen or GitHub Repo in the comments! 
Bonus Points : If the scroll speed changes based on a CSS :hover state.
Extra Credit : If you create a "Parallax" effect with multiple layers moving at different speeds.
Have fun!
articles.title: Daily Challenge #4 : The "Infinite" Scroll Illusion 🎞️

articles.author: kako-jun
articles.description:
My mother-in-law's house was hit by the 2024 Noto peninsula earthquake — intensity 7, the maximum on Japan's seismic scale. She watched a mountainside collapse in front of her. The neighborhood is mostly empty lots now. As the area slowly recovers, she started running a small guesthouse to support the local community. She needed to post monthly calendars on Instagram — which days are open, which are booked, which are closed.
I looked into how small businesses in Japan handle this, and fell into a rabbit hole.
If you look at the Instagram accounts of small businesses in Japan — ramen shops, Indian restaurants, hair salons, guesthouses — you'll notice something: they all post monthly calendar images.
Not Google Calendar embeds or booking widgets — just images. Hand-made, posted as photos.
 ○…
articles.title: My mother-in-law's post-earthquake guesthouse needed a calendar tool. Every result said Canva. So I built one.
